topic: AI workplace surveillance, algorithmic management, and self-fulfilling termination decisions

sources.title: Explainer: Algorithmic Management in the Workplace
sources.notes: Defines algorithmic management through pervasive worker data collection, real-time decision-making, automated evaluation, ratings, nudges, and penalties. This supports the episode's premise that a workplace system can monitor employees, score behavior, and shape conduct rather than merely observe it.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 — Artificial Intelligence Act
sources.publisher: Official Journal of the European Union
sources.notes: The EU AI Act treats certain AI systems used for employment, worker management, and access to self-employment as high-risk, reflecting the potential for automated systems to affect hiring, task allocation, monitoring, evaluation, promotion, and termination.

sources.title: Algorithms Need Management Training, Too
sources.notes: Documents the spread of algorithmic management beyond gig platforms into warehouses, call centers, retail, manufacturing, professional work, and public services. It describes workplace monitoring, automated discipline, and reported algorithm-driven firing, while arguing that crucial employment decisions should retain human judgment.

sources.title: Regulating Algorithmic Management: A Multi-Stakeholder Study of Challenges in Aligning Software and the Law for Workplace Scheduling
sources.notes: A 2025 multi-stakeholder study based on interviews with regulators, advocates, attorneys, managers, and workers. It finds that algorithmic scheduling systems influence legal compliance and worker well-being, supporting the story mechanism in which software does not simply predict outcomes but changes the organizational conditions that produce them.

sources.title: NLRB ruling on worker camera surveillance was 'nonsense,' DC Circuit says
sources.notes: Reports a real dispute over constant workplace camera monitoring and references a National Labor Relations Board general counsel position that electronic monitoring, including cameras and GPS, can chill protected worker activity. This grounds the episode's surveillance layer in an existing labor-law conflict.
